title: JavaScript: make pages interactive
summary: Make web pages respond to people: store data in variables, make decisions, repeat work with loops, write functions and change the page when someone taps or types. Every lesson has a short example you can change and run.
outcomes: Explain what JavaScript does and add it to a page with a <script> element
Use variables, data types, operators and if/else to calculate and make decisions
Store lists in arrays and work through them with loops
Write functions with parameters and return values
Find and change page elements with the DOM, and respond to clicks and typing
tools: Finish the HTML and CSS courses first. You need a phone or computer with a web browser: use the Try it yourself button in each lesson, Sololearn's free web code playground, or a free code-editor app such as Acode. On a computer, the free VS Code editor and the browser's developer console (press F12) are helpful but not required. No paid software is needed.

chapters.title: What JavaScript does
chapters.goal: Explain what JavaScript is for, add a script to a page and show a result on the page.

sections.heading: The third layer of a web page
sections.body:
HTML gives a page its structure and CSS gives it its look. **JavaScript** gives it behaviour: it can react when someone taps a button, check what they type, do calculations, show a countdown or change the page without loading a new one.

JavaScript is a real programming language. A program is a list of **statements**, instructions that run one after another from top to bottom. Each statement usually ends with a semicolon. In a web page, JavaScript runs inside the visitor's browser, on their own phone or computer. It can also run on servers, using tools such as Node.js, but this course is about the browser.

The example finds the paragraph with `id="msg"` and changes its text. You will learn exactly how in chapter 6; for now, change the words inside the quotes and run it again.

sections.heading: Where the <script> goes
sections.body:
JavaScript lives inside a `<script>` element. The browser runs a script **as soon as it reaches it**, while it is still reading the page, so a script can only change elements that come **before** it in the HTML. The simplest rule is to put your `<script>` just before `</body>`.

On a real site you will usually keep JavaScript in a separate file, such as `app.js`, and load it in the `<head>` with `<script src="app.js" defer></script>`. The `defer` attribute tells the browser to wait until it has read the whole page before running the file. It only works together with `src`; on a script written inside the page it does nothing.

Try moving the script in the example above the first paragraph and run it again. Nothing changes, because the paragraphs did not exist yet when the script ran.

sections.heading: console.log, alert and comments
sections.body:
Programmers often check their work with `console.log()`, which writes a message to the browser's **developer console**. Visitors never see it. On a computer, press F12 in Chrome, Edge or Firefox and open the **Console** tab to read it. The preview box in these lessons does not show the console, so our examples put their results on the page instead.

`alert()` shows a pop-up box with a message. The page waits until the box is closed, so it is fine for a quick test but annoying on a real site.

Comments are notes for people. In JavaScript, `//` starts a comment that lasts until the end of the line, and `/* ... */` can cover several lines.

points: JavaScript runs in the visitor's browser and can change the page after it has loaded
Statements run in order, from top to bottom
Put <script> just before </body>, or use an external file with defer in the head
console.log() writes to the developer console; alert() shows a pop-up box
// starts a one-line comment and /* */ wraps a longer one
mistakes: Running a script before the element it changes exists — place the script after that HTML.
Using curly quotes copied from a document or chat app — code needs straight quotes, ' or ".
Expecting console.log to show on the page — it only appears in the developer console.
Filling a real site with alert() boxes — show messages on the page instead.

chapters.title: Variables and data types
chapters.goal: Store values in variables with let and const and recognise the main data types.

sections.heading: Storing values with let and const
sections.body:
A **variable** is a named box for a value. You create one with a keyword, a name, an equals sign and a value:

- `const clubName = 'Coding Club';` creates a variable that cannot be given a new value later.
- `let members = 12;` creates a variable whose value can change: `members = members + 3;`

Use `const` by default and `let` when you know the value will change. You may see `var` in older code; new code uses `let` and `const`.

Names can contain letters, digits, `_` and `$`, but they cannot start with a digit or contain spaces or hyphens. JavaScript programmers usually write **camelCase**, such as `schoolFees` or `examDate`. Names are case-sensitive, so `score` and `Score` are two different variables.

sections.heading: Data types
sections.body:
Every value has a **type**. The main ones you will use are:

- **String**: text in quotes, such as `'Abuja'` or `"SS2"`. Single and double quotes both work.
- **Number**: whole or decimal numbers without quotes, such as `250` or `3.5`.
- **Boolean**: `true` or `false`, for yes-or-no facts.
- **undefined**: the value of a variable that has been created but not given a value yet.

The `typeof` operator tells you a value's type. **Template literals** are strings written between backticks instead of quotes. They let you drop values straight into the text with `${...}`, which is easier than joining pieces with `+`. On most phone keyboards the backtick is on the symbols page.

sections.heading: When numbers and text meet
sections.body:
The `+` operator does two different jobs. With two numbers it adds, but if either side is a string it **joins** them into a longer string. So `'5' + 3` gives `'53'`, not 8. Other maths operators, such as subtraction and multiplication, try to turn strings into numbers, so `'5' * 3` gives 15. This mix-up is one of the most common beginner bugs.

The fix is to turn text into a number on purpose with `Number()`: `Number('5') + 3` gives 8. This matters because anything a person types into a web page arrives as a string, even when it looks like a number. If the text is not a number at all, `Number('abc')` gives the special value `NaN`, which stands for not a number.

points: Use const by default, and let when the value must change
Strings are text in quotes, numbers have no quotes, and booleans are true or false
typeof tells you the type of a value
Template literals use backticks and ${} to put values inside text
+ joins strings, so convert text with Number() before adding
mistakes: Giving a const a new value, as in const total = 5; then total = 10; — this causes an error; use let if it must change.
Writing numbers in quotes, so '1000' + '500' gives '1000500' instead of 1500.
Using a variable before the line that creates it with let or const — this causes an error.
Using spaces or hyphens in names, such as school-fees — write schoolFees instead.

Then add 1 to the number of subjects with let and show the new sentence.

quiz.q: let price = 500; price = price + 200; What is the value of price now?
quiz.why: price starts at 500, and the second line stores 500 + 200 back into it.

quiz.q: const a = '10'; const b = 5; What is a + b?
quiz.why: a is a string, so + joins the two values as text instead of adding them.

quiz.q: What does typeof true give?
quiz.why: true and false are boolean values, so typeof gives the string 'boolean'.

quiz.q: const fee = 2000; fee = 2500; What happens?
opts: An error, because a const variable cannot be given a new value
fee stays 2000 and nothing else happens
quiz.why: const means the variable cannot be reassigned. Use let for values that change.

quiz.q: const name = 'Amaka'; What text does `Hi ${name}!` produce when it is written with backticks?
quiz.why: In a template literal, ${name} is replaced by the value of name.

chapters.title: Operators and if/else
chapters.goal: Calculate with operators, compare values and make decisions with if, else if and else.

sections.heading: Doing calculations
sections.body:
JavaScript can do all the maths a web page needs:

- `+` add, `-` subtract, `*` multiply, `/` divide
- `%` gives the **remainder** after dividing: `17 % 5` is 2
- `2 ** 3` raises 2 to the power of 3, which is 8

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just as in BODMAS, and brackets come first. `Math.round()` rounds to the nearest whole number. To show money neatly, `toLocaleString('en-NG')` adds commas, so `1500` is shown as `1,500`. Both `toLocaleString()` and `toFixed()` give back strings, so do your sums first and format the answer at the very end.

sections.heading: Comparing values
sections.body:
A **comparison** asks a question and gives a boolean answer, `true` or `false`:

- `===` equal to, and `!==` not equal to
- `>` greater than, `<` less than, `>=` at least, `<=` at most

Always use `===` rather than `==`. The triple version checks the type as well as the value, so `5 === '5'` is `false`, while the older `==` says `true`, which can hide bugs.

Combine questions with **logical operators**: `&&` (and) is true only if both sides are true, `||` (or) is true if at least one side is true, and `!` (not) turns true into false and false into true.

sections.heading: Making decisions with if, else if and else
sections.body:
An `if` statement runs a block of code only when its condition is true. `else` gives a block to run when the condition is false, and `else if` adds more conditions in between.

The browser checks the conditions **from top to bottom** and runs only the first block whose condition is true; it skips all the others. So when you check ranges, such as grades, start with the highest. If you checked `score >= 50` first, a score of 85 would stop there and get the wrong grade.

The example uses an imaginary school's grading scale. Change `score` to 85, 62, 50 and 30, and run it each time to test every branch.

points: % gives the remainder: 17 % 5 is 2
Use === and !== to compare; they check both value and type
&& needs both sides to be true; || needs at least one
if, else if and else check conditions from top to bottom and run only the first true branch
When checking ranges such as grades, test the highest range first
mistakes: Using = (which stores a value) instead of === (which compares) inside an if.
Checking score >= 50 before score >= 70, so a score of 75 gets the wrong grade.
Doing maths with the result of toFixed() or toLocaleString() — they give strings, so format only at the end.
Comparing numbers stored as text: '9' > '10' is true, because strings are compared character by character.

quiz.q: Eggs are packed in crates of 30. const eggs = 95; What is eggs % 30?
quiz.why: 95 eggs fill 3 crates (90 eggs) with 5 left over, and % gives the remainder.

quiz.q: let grade; const score = 75; if (score >= 50) { grade = 'C'; } else if (score >= 70) { grade = 'A'; } What is grade?
opts: 'C', because the first true condition wins
quiz.why: 75 >= 50 is true, so the first block runs and the else if is skipped. Check the highest range first.

quiz.q: What does 5 === '5' give?
quiz.why: === checks the type too: one side is a number and the other is a string, so they are not strictly equal.

quiz.q: const age = 16; const hasPermission = true; Which condition is true?
quiz.why: 16 >= 13 is true and hasPermission is true, so && gives true. The others are false.

quiz.q: What is 10 + 5 * 2?
quiz.why: Multiplication comes first: 5 * 2 is 10, and 10 + 10 is 20. Write (10 + 5) * 2 if you want 30.

chapters.title: Arrays and loops
chapters.goal: Store lists in arrays and use loops to work through every item.

sections.heading: Arrays: lists of values
sections.body:
An **array** stores a list of values in order, inside square brackets: `const subjects = ['Maths', 'English', 'Biology'];`

- Each item has a position called its **index**, and counting starts at **0**. So `subjects[0]` is `'Maths'` and `subjects[2]` is `'Biology'`.
- `subjects.length` is the number of items, here 3. The last item is always at `subjects[subjects.length - 1]`.
- `subjects.push('Chemistry')` adds an item to the end. This works even with `const`, because you are changing what is inside the array, not replacing the array.
- `subjects.includes('English')` gives `true` if the item is in the array.
- `subjects.join(', ')` joins all the items into one string.

sections.heading: Repeating with a for loop
sections.body:
A **loop** repeats code so you do not have to write it many times. The classic `for` loop has three parts inside its brackets:

`for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) { ... }`

1. `let i = 0` sets up a counter before the loop starts.
2. `i < items.length` is checked before every round, and the loop stops when it becomes false.
3. `i++` adds 1 to the counter after every round.

Inside the loop, `items[i]` is the current item. The condition uses `<`, not `<=`, because the last index is one less than the length. The example adds up a shopping list and builds a list on the page with `document.createElement`, which you will meet properly in chapter 6.

sections.heading: for...of and while loops
sections.body:
When you only need each item and not its index, `for...of` is shorter and harder to get wrong:

`for (const day of days) { ... }`

A `while` loop keeps going **as long as** its condition is true. It suits jobs where you do not know in advance how many rounds you need, such as counting the weeks it takes to save up for a textbook.

Make sure something inside a `while` loop changes its condition. If nothing does, the loop never ends and the page freezes. If that happens, reload the page and fix the code, which is one more reason to copy your work somewhere safe as you go.

points: Arrays hold ordered lists, and the first item is at index 0
array.length is the number of items; the last item is array[array.length - 1]
push() adds an item to the end of an array
for (let i = 0; i < list.length; i++) visits every index once
for...of gives you each item directly; a while loop needs a condition that eventually becomes false
mistakes: Writing i <= list.length, which runs one round too many and reaches an item that is undefined.
Forgetting that the first item is at [0], not [1].
A while loop whose condition never changes — the page freezes; make sure the loop updates a value it checks.
Starting a total with let total; instead of let total = 0; — adding to undefined gives NaN.
chapters.task: Make two arrays for a market list: five item names and their prices in naira. Use a for loop to show each item and price as a list on the page, and work out the total. Then use a while loop to find how many weeks it would take to save that total at ₦500 a week.

quiz.q: const subjects = ['Maths', 'English', 'Biology']; What is subjects[1]?
quiz.why: Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second item.

quiz.q: How many times does the body of for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) { ... } run?
quiz.why: i takes the values 0, 1, 2 and 3. When i becomes 4, the condition i < 4 is false and the loop stops.

quiz.q: const prices = [200, 300, 500]; let total = 0; for (const p of prices) { total = total + p; } What is total?
quiz.why: The loop adds each price in turn: 0 + 200 + 300 + 500 = 1000.

quiz.q: let total; for (const p of [100, 200]) { total = total + p; } Why is total NaN?
opts: total started as undefined, and undefined + 100 is NaN
Arrays cannot be used in for...of loops
quiz.why: A variable with no starting value is undefined, and maths with undefined gives NaN. Start with let total = 0;

quiz.q: let savings = 0; while (savings < 2000) { savings = savings + 500; } What is savings after the loop?
quiz.why: After four rounds savings is 2000, so savings < 2000 becomes false and the loop stops.

chapters.title: Functions
chapters.goal: Write functions with parameters and return values, and reuse them to keep code tidy.

sections.heading: Writing and calling a function
sections.body:
A **function** is a named block of code that does one job. You write it once and **call** it whenever you need that job done.

- `function greet(name) { ... }` defines a function called `greet`. The word inside the brackets, `name`, is a **parameter**: a placeholder for information the function needs.
- `greet('Chidi')` calls the function. The value you pass in, `'Chidi'`, is an **argument**.

A function does nothing until it is called, and you must include the brackets when you call it, even if it has no parameters. Functions let you split a big problem into small, named steps that you can test one at a time.

sections.heading: Returning a value
sections.body:
`return` sends a value back to the code that called the function, and the function stops there. Any code after `return` inside the function does not run. If a function has no `return`, calling it gives `undefined`.

A function can take several parameters, separated by commas. The order matters: the first argument goes into the first parameter, the second into the second, and so on. In the example, `change(price, paid)` must be called with the price first. Swap them and you get a negative answer.

Small helper functions, such as one that formats naira, keep the rest of your code short and easy to read.

sections.heading: Arrow functions and scope
sections.body:
You will often see a shorter way to write functions, called **arrow functions**: `const double = (n) => n * 2;` When the body is a single expression like this, its value is returned automatically. For longer arrow functions, use curly brackets and `return` as usual.

Variables created inside a function exist only inside it. This is called **scope**. It means two functions can each have their own variable called `total` without getting in each other's way, and code outside a function cannot reach its variables.

The example uses a function to count the days until an exam. The date in it is made up, so change it to test the code, and always check JAMB's official announcements for real exam dates.

points: A function is a named, reusable block of code; call it with its name and brackets
Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass in
return sends a value back and ends the function
A function without return gives undefined
Variables made inside a function cannot be used outside it
mistakes: Leaving off the brackets when calling, as in writing total instead of total() — the function does not run.
Forgetting return, then getting undefined instead of the answer.
Putting code after return and expecting it to run — return ends the function.
Passing arguments in the wrong order, such as change(paid, price) when the function expects change(price, paid).
chapters.task: Write a function called tip(bill, percent) that returns the tip in naira, rounded with Math.round(), and a second function that returns bill plus tip. Show the results for a ₦4,500 bill at 10% on the page, using a formatNaira helper.

quiz.q: function add(a, b) { return a + b; } What is add(2, 3) * 2?
quiz.why: add(2, 3) returns 5, and 5 * 2 is 10.

quiz.q: function half(n) { n / 2; } What does half(10) give?
quiz.why: The function works out n / 2 but never returns it, so the call gives undefined.

quiz.q: function change(price, paid) { return paid - price; } What does change(2000, 1500) give?
quiz.why: price becomes 2000 and paid becomes 1500, so it returns 1500 - 2000. The arguments were passed in the wrong order.

quiz.q: const square = (n) => n * n; What is square(4)?
quiz.why: A one-line arrow function returns its expression automatically: 4 * 4 = 16.

quiz.q: function setTotal() { const total = 50; } After calling setTotal(), code outside the function uses total. What happens?
opts: An error, because total only exists inside the function
It gives undefined with no error
quiz.why: total was declared inside the function, so it is out of scope outside it and JavaScript reports that it is not defined.

chapters.title: The DOM: find and change the page
chapters.goal: Use the DOM to find elements and change their text, styles and classes.

sections.heading: What the DOM is and how to find elements
sections.body:
When the browser reads your HTML, it builds the **DOM** (Document Object Model): a live family tree of objects, one for each element. JavaScript cannot change your HTML file, but it can change the DOM, and the page on screen updates straight away.

To change an element, you first find it:

- `document.querySelector('#total')` returns the **first** element that matches a CSS selector, or `null` if nothing matches.
- `document.querySelectorAll('.price')` returns **all** the matching elements, as a list you can loop over with `for...of`.

The selectors are the same ones you used in CSS: `#id`, `.class`, `p`, `nav a` and so on. Store an element in a `const` if you will use it more than once.

Eggs: ₦5,000

sections.heading: Changing text and adding elements
sections.body:
`textContent` reads or replaces the text inside an element. It treats everything as plain text, so it is the safe choice for showing anything, including what visitors type.

`innerHTML` reads or replaces the HTML inside an element, so tags in the string become real elements. It can be handy for content you wrote yourself, but never put visitors' text into `innerHTML`: someone could type HTML or code that then runs on your page.

You can also create new elements. `document.createElement('li')` makes a new element, you set its `textContent`, and `append()` adds it to the end of another element.

code.source: Club members

sections.heading: Changing styles and classes
sections.body:
Every element has a `style` property for setting CSS directly, as in `heading.style.color = 'darkgreen';`. CSS property names with hyphens become **camelCase** in JavaScript, so `background-color` becomes `backgroundColor` and `font-size` becomes `fontSize`. Values are strings and include the unit, such as `'28px'`.

For anything more than a quick change, it is neater to write the styles in CSS as a class and switch the class on and off with `classList`:

- `el.classList.add('highlight')` adds the class.
- `el.classList.remove('highlight')` removes it.
- `el.classList.toggle('highlight')` adds the class if it is missing and removes it if it is there.

This keeps the look in your CSS and the behaviour in your JavaScript.

points: The DOM is the browser's live model of the page, and JavaScript can change it
querySelector returns the first match or null; querySelectorAll returns every match
textContent sets plain text safely; innerHTML reads HTML tags, so never use it with text people type
In JavaScript, CSS names become camelCase: background-color becomes backgroundColor
classList.add, remove and toggle switch CSS classes on and off

Using an element that was not found — if querySelector gives null, check the spelling of the id or class.
Writing element.style.background-color — in JavaScript it is element.style.backgroundColor.
Using querySelector when you need every match — use querySelectorAll and a loop.

chapters.title: Events: build something interactive
chapters.goal: Respond to clicks and typing with event listeners and build a small interactive tool.

sections.heading: Responding to clicks
sections.body:
An **event** is something that happens on the page: a click or tap, a key press, text being typed. You tell an element what to do when an event happens with `addEventListener`:

`button.addEventListener('click', addOne);`

The first argument is the event's name, in lowercase and in quotes. The second is the **function to run**. Pass the function's name **without** brackets: `addOne`, not `addOne()`. With brackets, the function would run once straight away instead of waiting for the click. You can also write the function right there as an arrow function.

On a button, the `click` event fires for mouse clicks, finger taps and keyboard presses, so one listener covers phones and computers.

code.source:
Club attendance

Present today: 0

sections.heading: Reading what people type
sections.body:
To read an input box, use its `value` property. The value is **always a string**, even in a `type="number"` box, so convert it with `Number()` before you do maths.

The `input` event fires every time the value changes, so you can update a result while the person is still typing. The `change` event usually fires later, when they finish and leave the box.

Always plan for unexpected input. An empty box gives `''`, and `Number('')` is 0, which can quietly give wrong answers. In a `type="number"` box, the browser also gives `''` if what was typed is not a valid number. Check for empty boxes before calculating, and show a friendly message on the page.

sections.heading: Putting it together: a mini quiz
sections.body:
Now combine everything: variables, if/else, functions, the DOM and events. This mini quiz has one question and three answer buttons. It uses `querySelectorAll` to find all the buttons and a `for...of` loop to give each one a click listener.

Inside the listener, `button.textContent` tells you which answer was tapped. The code compares it with the correct answer, shows feedback with `textContent` and adds a class so that the chosen button turns green or red. The feedback also uses words, so it does not rely on colour alone.

For a full quiz, store several questions in an array and move to the next one after each answer. On a real page with a `<form>`, you would listen for the form's `submit` event and call `event.preventDefault()` to stop the page reloading. The preview box does not allow forms to be sent, so this example uses plain buttons.

code.source: What is the capital of Nigeria?

points: element.addEventListener('click', handler) runs the handler each time the element is clicked or tapped
Pass the function itself (handler), not the result of calling it (handler())
An input's value is always a string; convert it with Number() before doing sums
The input event fires every time the value changes, which is ideal for live results
Check for empty or invalid input and show a friendly message on the page
mistakes: Writing addEventListener('click', showTotal()) — this runs showTotal once straight away; pass showTotal without brackets.
Adding input values without converting them — '500' + '200' gives '500200'.
Using 'onclick' or 'Click' as the event name in addEventListener — the name is 'click', in lowercase.
Forgetting that an empty box counts as 0 after Number('') — check for empty input first.
chapters.task: Build a naira budget calculator for a club excursion: three labelled number boxes for transport, food and entry fees, and a paragraph that shows the total with toLocaleString('en-NG') as people type. Show a friendly message while any box is empty.

quiz.q: What is wrong with btn.addEventListener('click', sayHi());?
opts: sayHi runs once straight away, and its result is used as the listener; write sayHi without brackets
Arrow functions are required for click events
Nothing; this is the correct way to listen for clicks
quiz.why: The brackets call the function immediately. addEventListener needs the function itself, so it can call it on each click.

quiz.q: Two input boxes, a and b, contain 1500 and 500. What is a.value + b.value?
quiz.why: value is always a string, so + joins the two strings. Use Number(a.value) + Number(b.value) to get 2000.

quiz.q: Which event lets a total update while someone is still typing in a box?
quiz.why: input fires on every change to the value. change usually waits until the person leaves the box.

quiz.q: let count = 0; btn.addEventListener('click', () => { count++; out.textContent = count; }); After three taps on btn, what does out show?
quiz.why: Each tap runs the arrow function once, adding 1 to count and showing the new value.

quiz.q: A calculator does Number(box.value) * 50. Someone leaves the box empty. What happens, and why does it matter?
opts: Number('') is 0, so it quietly shows 0 instead of asking for a value
It shows an error message automatically
It shows NaN on every phone
The page refuses to run the code
quiz.why: An empty string converts to 0, so the answer looks real but is wrong. Check for empty input before calculating.

project.title: Add an interactive feature to your club page
project.brief: Add a working feature to the club page you built and styled in the HTML and CSS courses: either a five-question quiz about your club's subject, or a naira budget calculator that helps members plan an excursion. Keep your code in an external app.js file and show every result on the page.
steps: Choose the quiz or the budget calculator, and sketch on paper what people will see and do.
Add the HTML for the feature in a new section of index.html, with labels for any inputs and an empty element with an id for results.
Create app.js and load it in the head with <script src="app.js" defer></script>, or just before </body> without defer.
Store your data in variables and arrays: questions and correct answers, or cost items and their prices in naira.
Write small functions: one to calculate the score or total, and one to show the result on the page with textContent.
Connect buttons and inputs with addEventListener, using 'click' or 'input'.
Test with normal, empty and silly input, fix any bugs and style the new section with your existing CSS classes.
checklist: The feature works with taps on a phone and with a keyboard on a computer
Input values are converted with Number(), and empty input shows a friendly message
Results appear on the page, not only in the console or an alert
No personal data is collected, stored or sent anywhere
The code is split into small named functions with short comments
